analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug makers from paying generic and biosimilar makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2023 with three cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company is sued by a generic maker over a patent, the two sometimes settle by the brand-name company paying the generic maker to stay off the market longer — a practice called pay-for-delay, which keeps cheaper versions of a drug from reaching pharmacy shelves. This bill would make those deals illegal, with narrow exceptions such as a settlement that simply lets the generic sell the drug before the patent expires. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban, companies would have to file their settlement papers with the government, and violators could face civil penalties and lose the exclusive marketing window they get for being the first generic applicant.
analysis.who_benefits: People who fill prescriptions, since cheaper generic and biosimilar versions of drugs would reach the market sooner when patents are settled rather than bought off. Medicare, Medicaid, employers, and insurers who pay drug bills would also save, because generic entry typically drops a drug's price sharply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a brand-name drug or biologics maker to give anything of value to a generic or biosimilar applicant in exchange for limiting or delaying research, manufacturing, marketing, or sales of the competing product [S2] [S3].

Settlements are still allowed if the only consideration is the right to sell the drug before the patent or exclusivity expires, litigation expenses up to $7.5 million, or a promise not to sue — so genuine early-entry deals remain legal [S3].

Violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, with civil penalties up to three times the value transferred, enforceable exclusively by the Federal Trade Commission [S2] [S3].

Drug companies would have to file every settlement agreement with the FTC and Justice Department, and a company official would have to certify the filing includes all related agreements and even oral side promises — closing a loophole where side deals went unreported [S2] [S3].
A generic maker that takes part in a banned deal would forfeit its 180-day exclusivity period, removing the reward for joining a delay arrangement [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and biologics manufacturers, whose effective patent monopolies would end sooner, cutting into the extended high-price revenue that delay settlements currently protect. Generic makers would also lose the ability to collect payments for staying off the market.

drawbacks.text: The bill draws lines that could catch some agreements that genuinely benefit consumers: it responds by excluding deals where the payment is solely for real goods or services, and it lets the FTC write rules exempting agreements it finds procompetitive and good for consumers [S3].
Only the FTC could sue to enforce the ban, so individual companies and states could not bring their own cases, and the agency would have to act within six years of the settlement filing [S2] [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the tradeoff: patents exist to reward drug development, and banning nearly all paid patent settlements flatly, rather than case by case under existing antitrust law, risks discouraging some legitimate settlements — though the bill explicitly preserves existing antitrust law alongside the new rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for consumers: pay-for-delay deals keep brand-name prices in place for years after a generic could lawfully launch, and this bill bans the core mechanism while leaving genuinely procompetitive settlements on the table. The costs fall almost entirely on the pharmaceutical companies whose monopoly revenue is extended by those deals, with modest side effects — enforcement limited to one agency and a bright-line rule that may be blunter than antitrust case-by-case review. On balance the design is sound and the consumer case is strong; the bill's failure was a matter of legislative attention, not substance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on the day it was introduced, and to a Judiciary subcommittee three days later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the bill in the House on November 7, 2023, joined by cosponsors Sean Casten and Gerald Connolly [S1] [S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary Committee [S5].
On November 10, 2023, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025: the bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a Senate companion [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug and biologics makers are better off, because the pay-for-delay practice remains legal and they keep the ability to settle patent suits by paying generic makers to stay off the market; consumers continue to bear the higher prices that those deals preserve.

for.name: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill saw no committee action after its subcommittee referral.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill was sent to a subcommittee and stalled there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical brand-name manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Benefited from continued legality of pay-for-delay settlements; the industry has long opposed legislative bans on them, and no member of either party moved this bill forward.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor was a House Democrat — Perez plus Casten and Connolly, 3 of 216 House Democrats as cosponsors — and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill, but with no votes ever held the partisan shape is inferred rather than shown in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: These companies make money for years beyond a patent's practical life by paying generic challengers to stay off the market; the bill makes that payment illegal, so earlier generic entry would cut their extended monopoly revenue. Their loss is consumers' gain in the form of lower drug prices.

The bill removes a payday — settlements in which generic makers are paid to delay entry — but also protects them from the delay itself by making such deals unenforceable, and first-filers that join a banned deal would forfeit their 180-day exclusivity reward. On net it points them toward competing in the market rather than being paid to wait.

industries.industry: Health insurers, employers, and government drug payers
industries.note: Earlier generic and biosimilar entry sharply lowers what insurers, employers, Medicare, and Medicaid pay for prescriptions, so their interest runs with patients'.

The bill hands the FTC exclusive authority to enforce the ban, treat violations as unfair practices, seek civil penalties up to triple the value transferred, and exempt procompetitive deals by rule — a significant expansion of its drug-market antitrust toolkit.
